Question_text: A group of students performs an experiment to investigate the flow of oil at different temperatures. 200 cm³ of oil is heated gently and its temperature θ is recorded. The oil is then poured through a funnel into a second beaker, as shown in Fig. 1.1. The time t taken for the oil to flow through the funnel is recorded with a stopwatch.
image: Fig. 1.1 displays a diagram illustrating an experimental setup for observing oil flow. It shows a top beaker containing oil, with a funnel inserted into it. The funnel narrows and extends downwards, directing the oil into a second beaker placed below. All components are clearly labeled: 'beaker', 'oil', and 'funnel'.

Parts.part_text: State why it is important to stir the oil during heating.
Explain why the oil is heated gently.
The experiment is repeated for several values of θ. Values of θ and t are recorded in the table of Fig. 1.2.
Parts.image: Fig. 1.2 presents a table containing experimental data. It has two columns: 'θ/°C' (temperature in degrees Celsius) and 't/s' (time in seconds). The recorded data pairs are: 69, 13.69; 52, 14.97; 35, 17.34; 24, 21.16; 17, 25.16; 10, 28.85.

Parts.part_text: On Fig. 1.3, plot the graph of t/s on the y-axis against θ/°C on the x-axis. Start your graph from θ = 0°C and t = 12s. Draw the curved line of best fit.
Parts.image: Fig. 1.3 shows an empty graph grid with labeled axes. The x-axis represents 'θ/°C' and starts from 0. The y-axis represents 't/s' and starts from 12. The grid is extensive, designed for plotting the data from Fig. 1.2 and drawing a line of best fit.

Parts.part_text: Estimate the time taken for oil at 80 °C to flow through the funnel.
State the maximum reading on a standard laboratory liquid-in-glass thermometer that is suitable for this experiment.
Explain why it is not possible to repeat a reading immediately after it is taken.

Tick two boxes to show which of the following will make the experiment more accurate. using a more sensitive thermometer; using two people to take the measurements; using a thicker oil; using a larger range of readings; pouring the oil quickly after taking its temperature

Question_text: Fig. 2.1 shows a wooden metre rule with small holes drilled through it. The metre rule is suspended from the hole at 5.0 cm so that it can swing freely, as shown in Fig. 2.2. The rule is made to swing from side-to-side and the time T for one complete swing is determined.
image: Fig. 2.1 displays a wooden metre rule, marked from 0 to 100, with several small holes drilled along its length, notably at the 'holes' section. Fig. 2.2 illustrates the metre rule suspended from one of these holes (specifically, the one at 5.0 cm according to the text), allowing it to swing freely from side to side, indicating its use as a physical pendulum.

Parts.part_text: Describe three experimental techniques used to obtain an accurate value for T.

The distance d between a hole and the zero end of the rule is varied, by suspending the rule from different holes. The time T is determined for each value of d. The results are recorded in the table of Fig. 2.3.
Parts.image: Fig. 2.3 shows a table with two columns: 'd/cm' (distance from the zero end in centimeters) and 'T/s' (time for one complete swing in seconds). The recorded data pairs are: 5.0, 1.61; 10.0, 1.57; 20.0, 1.52; 30.0, 1.58; 40.0, 1.91.

Parts.part_text: Describe how T varies with d.
Suggest the value of T for d = 95.0 cm.
Suggest why T was not measured for d = 50.0 cm.

Question_text: The efficiency of a motor is measured using the apparatus shown in Fig. 3.1. When the motor is switched on, the string winds round the pulley and the load is lifted. Six students measure the time t taken for the load to be lifted a height h of 1.0 m.
image: Fig. 3.1 illustrates an experimental setup to measure motor efficiency. A motor is positioned horizontally, connected to a power supply. A string is wound around a pulley attached to the motor's shaft. This string then passes over a second, fixed pulley mounted on a stand at a height h = 1.0 m. The string continues downwards, attached to a 'load' resting on the ground. Labels include 'pulley', 'motor', 'string', 'h = 1.0 m', 'load', and 'to power supply'. The diagram is labeled 'not to scale'.

Parts.part_text: The times recorded are 4.47 s, 4.53 s, 4.39 s, 4.44 s, 5.92 s, 4.61 s.
The result of 5.92 s is discarded. Suggest why this result is very much larger than the others.
Calculate the average time tav of the other results. Considering the variation in the students’ results, give your answer to an appropriate number of significant figures. Show your working.
The efficiency E of the motor is given by the relationship E = (2 x 10^2) / (3 x t_av) %. Use this relationship to calculate E.
Describe one way in which the students can measure h accurately.

Question_text: A student performs an experiment using optical pins to find the effect of a circular block, made of transparent plastic, on parallel rays of light. Fig. 4.1 shows the circular plastic block on a sheet of white paper. The student draws round the block with a sharp pencil. The student also draws three parallel lines up to the block before starting the experiment.
